prose:d-2-tanzania-93bef4: Tanzania operates one of the more mature national health management information systems on the African continent, consolidating routine facility reporting across all levels with programme data from areas such as HIV, malaria, immunisation, and maternal and child health. It demonstrates how a large, geographically diverse country can consolidate multiple programme data streams into a coherent national information system, and offers lessons on data-quality governance, subnational capacity building and the management of facility reporting burden.
prose:d-2-uganda-d83254: Uganda's national health management information system, managed by the Ministry of Health, provides aggregate reporting across the public health system and has progressively integrated community health worker reporting, logistics data and surveillance. Uganda has also participated in piloting computable decision logic derived from WHO SMART Guidelines. The example is notable for the integration of community-level data into national aggregates and for early evidence on operationalising internationally developed computable guidance in a national system.
prose:d-2-united-kingdom-england-a7ab86: England governs pharmaceutical decision support centrally — providing interaction checking, allergy alerting and dosage guidance to prescribing systems across primary and hospital care — and operates a national terminology service hosting the SNOMED CT UK Edition and the dictionary of medicines and devices. It demonstrates how centrally governed pharmaceutical knowledge and terminology can be deployed through standardised interfaces to a diverse ecosystem of consuming systems, reducing duplicated maintenance and improving consistency of medication-safety guidance.
prose:d-2-united-states-f02f9f: The United States illustrates centralised knowledge governance with distributed consumption through the CDC immunisation decision-support logic (CDSi), consumed by a diverse ecosystem of immunisation systems and clinical applications [cdc-cdsi], and population-scale syndromic surveillance (BioSense) that draws on clinical data already generated at the point of care [cdc-nssp]. Both illustrate the governance of shared capability across a highly decentralised system with multiple jurisdictional authorities.
prose:d-3-european-union-and-european-ec: The European Surveillance System (TESSy) is a regional platform through which member states submit standardised communicable-disease surveillance data to the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control for regional analysis and international reporting [ecdc]. It demonstrates how a supranational authority can operate shared surveillance infrastructure across sovereign jurisdictions with diverse national systems, and offers lessons on cross-border data-sharing governance, indicator standardisation and the management of variation in case definitions within a common framework.
prose:d-3-who-smart-guidelines-pilot-imp: Several countries — including Ethiopia, the Philippines and Uganda — have piloted the deployment of L3 computable decision logic for areas such as antenatal care, HIV and immunisation within national health information systems. These pilots provide early evidence that internationally developed computable guidelines can be operationalised nationally, reducing the time and cost of adapting international clinical guidance for national deployment.
prose:e-40301a: Goal: core health data is captured once and reused reliably across programmes, services, and levels of care.
prose:e-ce763f: What the health system needs to be able to do: the health system needs authoritative, uniquely identified reference data — who people are, who provides care, where, with what products, and under what terms — held once and made available to every application component that needs it, rather than re-collected and reconciled in each. It needs that data to be well governed, current, and trustworthy, so that the systems built upon it can rely on it without duplicating or re-verifying it.
prose:e-d53f92: Unlike the goals that follow, this one has no mapping of its own. It is the foundation the other six draw on. Each of those mappings traces back to the same shared components — the client, health facility, and health workforce registries, the terminology service, the product registry, and the lifelong health record — and the recurrence of those components across goal after goal is the "capture once, use many times" principle made visible. The composition of that foundation, the minimum a country puts in place first, and how it matures over time are set out in the REDDHI framework in Section 2.2; the spreadsheets in this appendix show that foundation being reused, goal by goal.
prose:e-5534a6: Goal: a health workforce whose members are individually identifiable and verifiable, deployed where they are needed, paid reliably, and supported to maintain and extend their competencies across the course of their careers.
prose:e-f3eb0f: What the health system needs to be able to do: the system needs to know who its health workers are and what each is qualified and authorised to do, holding an authoritative record of identity, occupational classification, professional registration, and licensing status that clinical, administrative, financing, and regulatory systems can consistently rely on. It needs to see where workers are deployed and where shortages persist, so that staffing can be planned against population need rather than inferred from incomplete or paper-based records. And it needs to pay workers reliably, and to track the education, credentialing, and supervision through which competence is established and renewed over time.
prose:e-b1992f: How to read the mapping: the spreadsheet that follows traces each capability from the goal through stakeholder value, business capability, and application service to the DPI-H components and foundational-DPI dependencies that support it, and notes where each component is reused by other goals. Its most significant shared components are the Health Workforce Registry it centres on — itself a core foundational registry that other health goals also rely on — supported by the terminology service for occupational and qualification coding and the facility registry for linking workers to their sites of practice and mapping deployment, all resting on foundational-DPI identity, trust, payments, and single sign-on services. The workforce goal introduces no new DPI-H component; the operational systems that act on the registry — digital payroll, human-resource information systems, and learning-management and training-tracking applications — sit outside DPI-H and consume it rather than being defined by it.
prose:e-3d3f79: Goal: care that is informed by a person's full health history, guided by current evidence at the point of care, and coordinated across every provider, setting, and episode a person moves through.
prose:e-2238ff: What the health system needs to be able to do: the system needs to assemble a person's longitudinal record from the many places care is given and present it as a single coherent view, so that each encounter builds on what came before rather than starting afresh. It needs to make current, evidence-based protocols and decision support available to health workers as they make decisions, and to support the safe delegation of clinical tasks across cadres according to scope of practice. And it needs to coordinate care over time — referrals, transitions between settings, shared care plans, and follow-up — while tracking adherence and quality so that gaps and duplication can be seen and corrected.
prose:e-1325e8: How to read the mapping: the spreadsheet that follows traces each capability from the goal through stakeholder value, business capability, and application service to the DPI-H components and foundational-DPI dependencies that support it, and notes where each component is reused by other goals. Despite its breadth, the goal rests very largely on shared infrastructure other goals already require — the client registry to resolve a single patient identity across sources, the health workforce and facility registries to attribute care to verified providers and sites, the terminology service to keep clinical meaning consistent, and the lifelong health record as the shared longitudinal store every provider reads from and writes to. The genuinely new DPI-H component the goal introduces is the Clinical Decision Support Engine, which delivers context-aware, guideline-based recommendations at the point of care and has no direct equivalent in earlier reference architectures. The operational systems that carry out the work — point-of-care clinical applications, care-coordination and referral tools, electronic prescribing, laboratory and imaging systems — consume these shared components rather than being defined by DPI-H.
prose:e-405b00: Goal: every person has a verifiable digital health record that they can access and control, and that authorised providers can rely on across the places they seek care.
prose:e-ec7f55: What the health system needs to be able to do: the system needs to resolve each person to a single, verifiable identity and to assemble their longitudinal record so that it can be reached wherever care is given. It needs to let people see and govern who accesses their information, through consent that can be granted, recorded, and withdrawn. And it needs to assure the authenticity and integrity of records and of the people and institutions that contribute to them, so that a record can be trusted by a provider who did not create it.
prose:e-9cdd54: How to read the mapping: the spreadsheet that follows traces each capability from the goal through stakeholder value, business capability, and application service to the DPI-H components and foundational-DPI dependencies that support it, and notes where each component is reused by other goals. This goal is distinctive in introducing no new DPI-H component of its own: it is the goal the foundational shared-data layer exists to serve, realised through the client registry and the lifelong health record, supported by the workforce and facility registries for accountable, verified contribution and by the terminology service for consistent meaning, and resting on foundational-DPI trust services together with the cross-cutting consent and security properties addressed elsewhere in this guidance. The patient-facing applications through which people view and manage their records consume this foundation rather than being defined by DPI-H.
prose:e-0e6ccd: Goal: safe health products reach the people who need them, when and where they are needed, through a supply chain that is visible end to end and able to adapt when demand shifts.
prose:e-97c216: What the health system needs to be able to do: the system needs to forecast demand and plan supply against budgets and programme priorities, and to see stock levels and product movement from source to point of use. It needs to identify products, locations, suppliers, and individual batches consistently, so that an item can be traced through ordering, storage, transport, and dispensing, and recalled or removed when needs arise. And it needs to connect these flows to the rest of the health system — to facilities, to financing, and to the people who ultimately receive the products.
prose:e-73950f: How to read the mapping: the spreadsheet that follows traces each capability from the goal through stakeholder value, business capability, and application service to the DPI-H components and foundational-DPI dependencies that support it, and notes where each component is reused by other goals. The goal leans on shared infrastructure other goals already require — the health facility registry to locate every point in the network, the terminology service to standardise product and service codes, and the client registry where dispensing is traced to the individual — while the components specific to this domain are two reference registries: a Product Registry that lets products be identified and traced consistently across the network, and a Supplier Registry that records provenance and supplier accountability. The operational systems that run the supply chain — forecasting, order, warehouse, procurement, transport, and dispensing applications, including the tracking of individual batches and serial numbers — consume these shared registries rather than being defined by DPI-H.
prose:e-deab37:
Goal: mobilise, pool, and allocate health funds efficiently and equitably, purchase covered services transparently, pay providers and health workers reliably, and protect people from financial hardship when they seek care.

What the health system needs to be able to do: the system needs to define and publish what health services and products are covered under each scheme, enrol eligible individuals and households, and enable patients and providers to understand entitlements clearly — pairing machine-readable definitions with plain-language, multilingual, accessible explanations and assisted-access support. It needs to empanel and contract qualified facilities and health workers, establish transparent tariffs, fee schedules, and payment methods, verify eligibility and prior authorisation where required, and adjudicate claims against clinical coding rules and verifiable evidence of service delivery. And it needs to execute lawful, timely payments to facilities, suppliers, and health workers through public financial management, payroll, and digital payment systems while safeguarding public funds through internal controls, audit, anomaly detection, investigation, appeal mechanisms, and independent oversight.

How to read the mapping: the method is illustrated in the worked example in Section 2.4.2, and the spreadsheet that follows traces each financing capability from the goal through stakeholder value, business capability, and application service to the shared DPI-H reference components, foundational-DPI dependencies, and operational financing systems that together realise it. Reading the mapping requires keeping six architectural boundaries explicit:

  • Shared DPI-H reference components versus operational financing systems. Within the scope of DPI-H, the principal domain-specific shared reference component is the Benefits Package Registry, which publishes authoritative benefit package definitions, coverage parameters, and testable machine-readable reference rules. It does not determine person-specific eligibility, enrol beneficiaries, manage provider contracts, or adjudicate claims; those functions sit in operational systems outside DPI-H — Beneficiary Registries and enrolment platforms, Contract and Benefits Management Systems (CBMS), provider contracting and tariff systems, prior-authorisation and claims adjudication engines, and public financial management (PFM) systems — which consume the shared registries.
  • Canonical person identity versus scheme enrolment and individual eligibility. The Client Registry (anchored on foundational digital identity where available) resolves canonical person identity, but does not store scheme membership, premium or contribution status, social-protection exemptions, household contribution groupings, or benefit utilisation. Those records belong to operational beneficiary and enrolment systems (and cross-sector social-protection linkages under data-minimisation safeguards), which reconcile enrolment and claims records against the shared Client Registry identity to support person-specific eligibility determination and cross-scheme duplicate-enrolment checks.
  • Facility and workforce credentials versus provider empanelment and contracting. The Health Facility Registry and Health Workforce Registry establish authoritative facility and practitioner identity, licensing, service capability, and professional registration status. They do not establish provider empanelment, payer-provider contracts, service authorisation, or claim and payment eligibility; those are operational financing relationships managed in provider-contracting and CBMS platforms that reference authoritative facility and workforce identifiers.
  • Product and terminology references versus pricing, tariffs, and claims adjudication. The Product Registry and Terminology Service provide standardised identifiers and clinical codes for medicines, commodities, diagnoses, and procedures, but accurate pricing and reimbursement additionally require operational tariff schedules, payer-provider contracts, fee schedules, clinical coding and bundling rules, benefit limits, payment methods (such as capitation, case-based/DRG, or fee-for-service), executable claims logic, and adjudication systems that assess the sufficiency and provenance of service-delivery evidence.
  • Payment decisions and financial controls versus payment settlement rails. Foundational payment DPI, banking interfaces, and treasury rails initiate, settle, and reconcile monetary transfers, but they do not determine whether a payment is accurate, lawful, contractually compliant, or appropriately authorised. Decisions on benefit coverage, claim validity, provider contract compliance, and financial control sit in operational health-financing, PFM, budget, contract, attendance, and payroll systems, which authorise payments before instructing payment rails to move funds and which govern timely health-worker and provider remuneration beyond DPI-H.
  • Registry linkage versus comprehensive fraud and integrity governance. Linking claims and enrolment records to authoritative Client, Facility, Workforce, Product, Supplier, and Benefits Package registries supports integrity controls and helps detect duplicate enrolment or phantom entities, but registry linkage does not by itself prevent fraud, corruption, false claims, upcoding, collusion, or leakage. Safeguarding health funds requires combining registry verification with operational clinical and financial audit, anomaly detection, investigation workflows, graduated sanctions, beneficiary and provider appeal mechanisms, internal financial controls, and independent oversight.
